alternatives.option: Ship meetings with channel labels only until a diarizer is measured
alternatives.tradeoff: Avoids shipping unmeasured attribution; drops a requested feature.

decisions.consequences: Two artifacts per meeting at native rate, roughly doubling meeting storage. Diarization weights are an explicit acquisition step, because notices for the embedder and clusterer are component-specific. Attribution shown as unverified is the normal state the transcript view must explain. Speakers without centroids get no cross-recording proposal. If measured diarization error exceeds its approved range, the shipped default for meetings becomes channel labels with diarization off and user-enablable, which changes a default rather than removing the feature and never gates an imported model.
decisions.reconsider_when: F5 shows the API exposes per-segment evidence, evaluation shows centroid distance is monotone with correctness allowing a derived threshold with its calibration curve, a notice blocks integration, or mixed-stream diarization matches channel-separated results.

decisions.title: History: append-only results over identified runs, full-text search, tombstones with generation tokens
decisions.choice: History lists recordings, each expandable into its processing runs and their result chains. Search is FTS5 over result text with bm25 ranking and snippets, and retained context is not indexed. Playback uses the sealed artifact. Reprocessing creates a run and inserts results; nothing is mutated, and a user-movable pointer selects the displayed run. Deletion sets a tombstone, increments a generation counter and signals cancellation; every worker carries recording id and generation from admission and commits in one transaction that aborts if the row is missing, tombstoned or at a different generation. Hard deletion happens when the last lease releases or at the next launch sweep.
decisions.rationale: A late worker response cannot recreate a deleted recording only if the existence check and the insert are the same transaction; any check-then-insert has a window. The generation counter covers delete-then-recreate at the same identifier. Organizing the list by run is what makes reprocessing through a different speech model or diarizer comparable, since each run names its inputs, its models and its code revisions.

alternatives.option: Hard delete immediately and let workers fail
alternatives.tradeoff: No tombstone bookkeeping; a constraint violation becomes the race outcome and scratch files are orphaned.

alternatives.option: Cancel workers and wait for acknowledgement before deleting
alternatives.tradeoff: No tombstone state; the user's delete blocks on a worker mid-window, and a hung worker blocks it indefinitely.

alternatives.option: Overwrite results on reprocessing
alternatives.tradeoff: One result per recording and a simpler list; comparing a new model against the old becomes impossible.

decisions.consequences: Deleted recordings hold disk until leases release, so the interface says deleting rather than claiming reclaimed space. FTS triggers must handle result deletion, covered by tests. A recording with several runs needs a detail view that makes each run's inputs and outputs obvious.
decisions.reconsider_when: Result rows dominate database size, which argues for storing older results compressed or on disk.

decisions.title: Desktop behavior: menu bar surface, software input gain, and media control only through an owning player integration
decisions.choice: An NSStatusItem shows state, current mode, recent results and settings. Microphone level is software gain on captured buffers by default, with metering and a clipping indicator; setting the input device's hardware volume is opt-in and restored only if the current value still equals the value the app set. Automatic pausing and automatic resumption both require a MediaPlayerAdapter that queries an identified player, issues a one-way pause to it, and observes the transition to paused; only such an owned pause is resumed automatically, and only while the player still reports paused. For a player with no adapter the app takes no automatic action: the panel and menu offer Pause media and Resume playback as explicit user actions, labeled as a media-key toggle whose recipient and effect the app cannot confirm.
decisions.rationale: The specification states that automatic restoration needs an integration identifying the affected player and confirming the pause transition, and that opting in does not remove that condition. The previous revision still posted a play-pause key automatically when the default output device reported a running client, and REVIEW_NOTES records why that is unsafe in both directions: a global toggle can start a paused player while an unrelated client keeps the device active, so the claimed worst case of nothing happening is false. Restricting automatic action to a one-way pause addressed to an identified player removes that outcome while keeping the convenience where the app can own it. Software gain changes no system setting, so the common case has no restore obligation.

alternatives.option: Post the play-pause key automatically when the output device is running
alternatives.tradeoff: Covers every player with no adapters; the key is a toggle, so it can start playback the user stopped.

alternatives.option: Opt-in automatic resume gated on device idle and elapsed time
alternatives.tradeoff: Nothing to click after recording; the conditions establish neither recipient nor transition, which the specification rules out.

alternatives.option: Private MediaRemote framework for playback state and control
alternatives.tradeoff: Accurate per-application state without per-player adapters; an undocumented interface that can break on any OS update and complicates notarization posture.

alternatives.option: Do not touch media playback at all
alternatives.tradeoff: Nothing to get wrong; leaves background audio bleeding into recordings, which the requirement asks to address.

decisions.consequences: Automatic pausing now covers only players with an adapter, so the out-of-the-box behavior is a menu action for unsupported players and the coverage grows one integration at a time. Each adapter needs its own automation permission and maintenance; a broken adapter degrades to the manual action. The clipping indicator surfaces hardware-side clipping that software gain cannot rescue.
decisions.reconsider_when: A supported system API supplies playing-application identity and pause confirmation without per-player integrations.

decisions.title: Shortcuts: distinct toggle and push-to-talk bindings, evidence-based stuck-key recovery, no duration cap
decisions.choice: A single ShortcutRegistrar owns a session-level consuming CGEventTap handling keyDown, keyUp and flagsChanged. Toggle and push-to-talk are separate bindings; a combination may be bound to at most one of them, validated at bind time. Toggle acts on keyDown. Push-to-talk starts on keyDown and finalizes on keyUp, with an optional per-binding tap-to-lock where a keyUp within 250 ms by default latches recording until the next press. Lost key-up is recovered from tap-disabled, screen lock and sleep notifications, and a 1 Hz poll of the physical key state. There is no maximum recording duration. Per-mode bindings are toggle or push-to-talk bindings with a mode attached. kCGEventTapDisabledByTimeout re-enables the tap. Without the tap, toggle falls back to Carbon RegisterEventHotKey and push-to-talk is unavailable with an explanation.
decisions.rationale: Overloading one binding with a hold discriminator leaves the first hold window undefined and makes a short press ambiguous. Polling the physical key state addresses the real problem, a key-up the tap never delivered, with evidence about that key, while a maximum-hold watchdog would truncate valid speech and act as the recording-duration limit the specification prohibits.

alternatives.option: One binding with a hold discriminator
alternatives.tradeoff: One combination to configure; the first hold window has undefined behavior and a dropped event changes the meaning of a press.

alternatives.option: Carbon RegisterEventHotKey only
alternatives.tradeoff: No Accessibility permission and reliable consumption; no key-up, so push-to-talk cannot exist.

alternatives.option: NSEvent global monitors only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple API with no tap lifecycle; events cannot be consumed, so the hotkey also reaches the foreground application.

alternatives.option: A maximum hold watchdog
alternatives.tradeoff: Guarantees a stuck key eventually stops recording; truncates a genuinely long push-to-talk recording.

decisions.consequences: The app sits on the keyboard event path, so its handler must stay fast or the tap is disabled by timeout, which the re-enable path treats as a monitored condition. Users configure two shortcuts instead of one. The key-state poll runs only while a push-to-talk recording is active. Capture starting at the trigger (D-006) means a very short press still produces a short recording rather than nothing.
decisions.reconsider_when: A supported API provides global hotkeys with key-up, or the poll proves unreliable for remapped or external keyboards.

decisions.title: Residency under a declared budget covering every model kind and the non-model floor
decisions.choice: Budget the application at 8 GB peak on the 16 GB target, counting the app and all its services. Slots are speech-primary, speech-preview, generation and diarization, at most one occupant each, unloaded after ten idle minutes, with admission checking the summed declared or measured footprint before starting a job. A preview-class installation qualifies for the speech-preview slot only if its declared footprint is under 400 MB. Non-model ingest memory is bounded by the session and credit limits in D-004 and D-018 and is counted at a stated ceiling of 200 MB. Diarization does not run concurrently with generation under the declared numbers. Activation of a pairing exceeding the budget is refused with the arithmetic shown, the refusal stating whether its numbers are measured or declared, and an override available. Once F1 and F5 descriptors exist, admission uses measured peak resident size and Metal heap peak.
decisions.rationale: The specification forbids artificial quotas and requires honest reporting of limits, which differs from ignoring the ceiling: swap on a 16 GB machine turns a latency problem into a system-wide stall. The previous revision counted only three model kinds and treated ingest memory as invisible, so a preview model and several concurrent imports could sit outside the budget they were supposed to respect. Declared weight sizes omit runtime workspaces, Metal allocations and service overhead, so a refusal computed from them can deny a pairing that would have worked; labeling the basis and keeping the override means the policy never becomes a limit the user cannot see through.

alternatives.option: Load on demand with no residency limit
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and fastest where memory allows; a large pairing plus a browser drives the target machine into swap.

alternatives.option: Count only the large models and treat preview and ingest as free
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler arithmetic; the components whose footprints are least known sit outside the accounting.

alternatives.option: Keep selected models resident permanently
alternatives.tradeoff: Lowest per-run latency; several gigabytes held while the app idles in the menu bar.

alternatives.option: Rely on memory pressure notifications alone
alternatives.tradeoff: Adapts to real conditions; reacts after the stall has started.

decisions.consequences: First use after idle pays a model load shown as a loading state. A meeting's diarization and its notes run are sequential under the declared numbers. The preview slot is unavailable on a machine whose budget it would break, which selects a lower preview rung. Until descriptors exist the budget is arithmetic that can be wrong in either direction, which the refusal text says.
decisions.reconsider_when: Measured residency from F1 and F5 differs materially from declared sizes, or the app runs on machines where the ceiling does not bind.

decisions.title: Egress control enforced by the service sandbox, with no fallback outside the boundary
decisions.choice: Inference and decoding run in services whose sandbox omits the network client entitlement, so the system denies outbound connections. That boundary has no fallback. Downloads happen only through ModelDownloader on explicit user action, restricted to an allowlist of model hosts and writing only into staging. Runtimes receive absolute local paths through one of the three access mechanisms in D-003, are constructed with acquisition disabled, and a static check fails the build if a runtime is constructed through an initializer that can download. The external decoder runs as a child of the sandboxed decode service, is off by default, and is disabled entirely by the strict offline setting. The shipped claim is that inference and decoding run in processes the system denies network access, evidenced by an in-service connection attempt that fails; build checks, dependency-closure checks and a symbol scan corroborate that claim and do not establish it, because RESEARCH states a symbol scan cannot establish that a process lacks network access.
decisions.rationale: The specification requires that audio, transcripts and context stay on the Mac and that model loading not trigger downloads, and RESEARCH notes a diarization runtime whose default initialization may download models. The previous revision pre-wrote a narrowed claim for an unsandboxed service if the sandbox could not load a runtime, which made a loader detail able to weaken the local-only property during routine operation, and the review was right that the weaker evidence is the scan RESEARCH rejects. Fixing the boundary and varying the runtime instead puts the choice where the evidence is: three access mechanisms, one of which needs no entitlement beyond the service's own container, then the alternative adapter, then a product-owner escalation.

alternatives.option: Unsandboxed service with a narrowed claim when loading fails
alternatives.tradeoff: Any runtime can be used; the offline property during normal use rests on evidence RESEARCH says cannot establish it.

alternatives.option: Symbol scan plus a network-denied session test only
alternatives.tradeoff: No entitlement work; cannot cover system frameworks or dynamically loaded code.

alternatives.option: Allow runtimes to fetch missing models
alternatives.tradeoff: Better first run with no model manager; makes network access a side effect of loading a model.

alternatives.option: Ship no downloader and require manual placement
alternatives.tradeoff: Strongest guarantee and least code; makes first run considerably harder and pushes users toward downloading models through less careful means.

decisions.consequences: Entitlement sets are part of the signed product and a missing one fails closed. A runtime that cannot load inside the boundary is not shipped for that model kind, which is a runtime-selection cost rather than a contract change. The decoder is constrained only if sandbox inheritance holds; F2 tests that directly, and if it does not hold the decoder stays off by default with the trust transfer stated in its settings.
decisions.reconsider_when: F2 shows a required model kind has no adapter that loads inside the boundary, which is a specification question for the product owner rather than an implementation fallback.

decisions.title: Processing runs as the provenance spine, with a dependency table that can name non-result inputs
decisions.choice: processing_runs sits between recordings and results. Every result belongs to a run, names its primary input through primary_input_result_id, and records every other input in result_dependencies(result_id, input_kind, input_id, role) with input_kind in {result, speaker_assignment_revision, audio_artifact}. Recognition results are chain roots carrying the speech installation; a diarization result carries the diarizer installation and names its audio artifacts; a notes result has the transcript as primary input and dependency rows for the diarization result and the assignment revision. A recording may hold several recognition and several diarization results. Results are immutable after insert, enforced by a trigger.
decisions.rationale: A recording cannot have exactly one source transcript while also being re-recognizable through a different speech model, so parentage is a foreign key rather than an inference from timestamps. A single result-typed input column was not enough once notes entered the graph: a note depends on an assignment revision, which is not a result and had no representable role, so the previous schema could not hold what D-037 said it held and the verification invariant asserting it was unsatisfiable. A typed input kind keeps the graph extensible when a later result kind depends on another entity.

alternatives.option: Keep one transcript per recording and forbid re-recognition
alternatives.tradeoff: The simplest graph; removes reprocessing through another speech model.

alternatives.option: Single result-typed parent, other inputs only in the manifest
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer rows; provenance queries cannot join on the second input, so History cannot show which assignment revision a note used without parsing manifests.

alternatives.option: Fixed nullable columns for transcript, diarization and assignment inputs
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheaper joins; a new result kind with a different dependency needs a migration and another column.

alternatives.option: Attach model ids to results and infer parentage by timestamp
alternatives.tradeoff: No new table; parentage becomes a guess that breaks whenever two runs overlap.

decisions.consequences: More joins in History queries and a detail view that presents runs with their inputs. Reprocessing gains a clear entry stage. The FTS index carries results from every run, so search can return two recognitions of the same audio, which the result rows disambiguate.
decisions.reconsider_when: Users never re-recognize or re-diarize, which would make the run table pure overhead, though the same structure is what makes translations and notes attributable.

decisions.title: Crash-safe capture through an fsynced chunk journal with a stated commit order and an idempotent finalization
decisions.choice: Capture writes fixed-period chunks, two seconds by default, of headerless native-rate PCM, each written to a part file, fsynced, renamed, with the directory fsynced. The sealer cycle per chunk is: encode; append packet bytes to the CAF data chunk; fsync the CAF file; append a data record and fsync it; delete covered journal chunks and fsync the directory. A data record carries magic, kind, record and chunk sequence, first packet index, packet count, frames per packet, byte offset and length, per-packet byte sizes as varints, and a CRC32. Finalization commits sealing: encode and commit every remaining chunk first, then append the pakt chunk and fsync, then patch the data chunk size and fsync, then hash and append a seal record naming the last data record, the pakt offset, the file length and the SHA-256, and fsync, then commit the rows. Recovery accepts the durable prefix by CRC and byte range; if it ends in a matching seal record the artifact is finalized, otherwise recovery truncates to the end of the last accepted data record, commits surviving journal chunks through the ordinary cycle, and runs finalization again.
decisions.rationale: Encoded bytes are fsynced before the record that names them, so recovery never builds a table over data that never reached disk, and per-packet sizes are present because an ALAC packet table cannot be reconstructed from a count and an offset. The previous revision described recovery as rebuilding the table and then appending surviving chunks, which leaves the table stale, and said nothing about a crash during the table write, the size patch or the hash. Ordering surviving chunks before the table, and making the seal record the commit point, gives a sequence that converges when repeated: any partially written table or patch is removed by truncating to the accepted prefix, and every step derives from records the application wrote and fsynced.

alternatives.option: Rebuild the table and then append surviving chunks
alternatives.tradeoff: One pass over the index; the finalized table does not describe the appended packets.

alternatives.option: Treat the presence of a pakt chunk as the commit signal
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra record; a torn pakt write is indistinguishable from a complete one.

alternatives.option: Write the container directly and rely on it being recoverable
alternatives.tradeoff: No journal, no sealer, no extra fsyncs; recovery rests on an untested property of a format that stores its table at the end.

alternatives.option: Keep raw PCM as the only durable form until the run completes
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest recovery; transient storage equals the full raw recording.

decisions.consequences: Two fsyncs per chunk period per stream, plus three in finalization, and a recovery path that must stay idempotent under repeated crashes, which F3 tests directly. Roughly a 30-second window of journal files sits alongside the artifact during long captures, bounded by the sealer rule in D-004. If F3 shows reconstruction can be invalid, the structural fallback is to retain chunks until the finalized artifact decodes and hashes.
decisions.reconsider_when: F3 shows a loss bound or a reconstruction failure the product cannot live with, or a container format with an incrementally durable index removes the need for a separate journal.

decisions.title: A state-indexed recovery contract with an explicit durability ordering rule
decisions.choice: Every non-terminal run state has an authoritative recovery transition, listed in the data lifecycle and covering arming, capturing, sealing, recognizing, diarizing, refining, rewriting, noting and delivering, plus the case of a completed meeting with no notes run. Before the sealing commit, ownership and disposition live in the session directory's fsynced manifest, and recovery honors that disposition. The ordering rule is written down: a durable record of intent precedes an externally visible irreversible effect, while a locally idempotent effect is followed by its commit. Recovery may complete deterministic stages such as refining and finalization, and never resumes generation, diarization or delivery without user action.
decisions.rationale: A recovery sweep that covers only some states leaves the rest to whichever test author reaches them first, which is the deferral the specification prohibits. Naming the ordering rule makes new stages easy to place correctly. Recording pre-commit disposition in the manifest is what makes a cancellation issued before the History row exists survive a crash. Not starting a notes run automatically follows the same rule that keeps recovery from consuming a model without the user asking.

alternatives.option: Discard any run in flight at a crash
alternatives.tradeoff: One rule and no partial state; throws away a completed recognition because the app crashed during a rewrite.

alternatives.option: Resume every in-flight run automatically
alternatives.tradeoff: Least user friction; re-runs generation the user may no longer want and risks re-delivering into whatever is now focused.

alternatives.option: Ask the user at launch what to do with each interrupted run
alternatives.tradeoff: No wrong default; a dialog at every launch after a crash invites blind dismissal.

decisions.consequences: Recovery does deterministic work automatically and stops at anything that consumes a model or touches another application, so a crashed meeting leaves a Generate action rather than a note. Behavior tables must cover every state, and the crash-injection suite asserts against them.
decisions.reconsider_when: A new stage appears whose effects are neither externally visible nor idempotent, which would need a rule of its own.

decisions.title: Permissions as a capability-by-state matrix
decisions.choice: A matrix over capability, run state and active adapter replaces any single revocation outcome. Losing microphone or an active system-audio stream terminates capture; losing Accessibility affects insertion, readback, target revalidation and shortcut consumption and not recognition; losing Input Monitoring affects shortcuts; losing browser automation affects URL predicates; losing player automation removes that player's adapter and drops it to the manual action in D-025; losing Screen Recording ends screen context and system-audio capture while leaving microphone capture running. Denial at launch, revocation during work and restoration each have a defined effect, and restoration is reported once.
decisions.rationale: Mapping every revocation to a capture failure would end a valid recording because the user changed a delivery permission during recognition, and would report a lost shortcut permission as an audio failure. Capabilities serve different stages, so their loss belongs at those stages.

alternatives.option: One global failure state
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple to implement and explain; stops work that is still valid and misreports the cause.

alternatives.option: Ignore revocation until the capability is next used
alternatives.tradeoff: No mid-run interruption; the user gets a confusing failure later with no connection to the change they made.

decisions.consequences: The matrix is longer than a rule, is directly testable, and becomes part of the approved behavior tables. Each capability needs a probe and a change notification path. Losing Accessibility mid-delivery makes revalidation impossible, so the attempt holds rather than posting blind.
decisions.reconsider_when: A capability appears whose loss affects several stages differently enough that the matrix needs a third dimension beyond adapter identity.

decisions.title: One artifact lease protocol after commit, session-directory ownership before it, reclamation by holder liveness
decisions.choice: A leases table records holder process id, holder process start time, connection identifier, artifact, acquisition time and heartbeat. Acquiring a lease requires the recording row to exist, be untombstoned and match the expected generation. Workers, the audio player, exports and every retention policy acquire leases. A lease is reclaimable only when its holder is provably gone, meaning the process no longer exists or its start time differs, or its XPC connection has been invalidated; the heartbeat is displayed as progress and never on its own authorizes reclamation. Retention skips recordings with a live lease and retries on the next pass. Before the sealing commit no row exists, so ownership is the session directory, held by one RunActor, with cancellation and deletion expressed as a disposition in the fsynced manifest. Discarding audio is a distinct audio_discarded state that disables playback, re-recognition and re-diarization while leaving text reprocessing available.
decisions.rationale: One protocol for every consumer removes a class of race rather than one instance. Defining staleness by holder liveness rather than by a heartbeat interval is what keeps a suspended app or a worker stalled on a slow disk from having its artifact deleted underneath it: a missed heartbeat is evidence about scheduling, while a dead process is evidence about ownership. Naming the session directory as the pre-commit unit of ownership closes the gap where the protocol presupposed a row that capture does not create until sealing.

alternatives.option: Reclaim leases after a heartbeat timeout
alternatives.tradeoff: Recovers from any stall without inspecting processes; deletes an artifact a live but delayed holder is still using.

alternatives.option: Create a placeholder recording row at arming
alternatives.tradeoff: One ownership mechanism throughout; History gains rows for recordings that may never exist.

alternatives.option: Retention as immediate deletion with best-effort cancellation
alternatives.tradeoff: Policies always run on schedule; a race with an admitted job produces a timing-dependent outcome.

alternatives.option: Reference counting in memory only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheaper than a table; counts vanish on a crash, so recovery cannot tell which artifacts were in use.

decisions.consequences: Every consumer of a committed artifact acquires a lease, including playback. Pre-commit work has a different ownership mechanism, so recovery has two paths to implement and test. A lease held by a process that is alive but wedged blocks retention until the user or the hang detector terminates it, which is reported rather than forced.
decisions.reconsider_when: Lease contention delays retention long enough to matter, which would argue for pausing playback and preempting batch work in place of deferring.

decisions.title: Measurements precede the boundaries they can invalidate, with approved ranges, basis and actions
decisions.choice: Five evidence gates (F1 runtime harness including its comparison arm and preview arm, F2 service isolation, F3 capture durability and sealer behavior, F4 insertion matrix, F5 diarizer adapter inventory) run before the boundaries that depend on them. Each gate's range, the basis of that range and the action attached to a failure are recorded in verification and approved under D-035 before the gate runs. These govern shipped defaults; none gates a compatible model a user imports. Task-level phases are produced after design acceptance.
decisions.rationale: Several decisions depend on properties nothing has measured, and scheduling those after the ports and schema that depend on them would let a negative result invalidate work already built on it. Recording a range with its basis and its action is what makes a result decide something; a measurement with no attached consequence is a number in a report, and a range with no recorded basis cannot be argued with. The previous revision carried ranges whose origin was not stated and one criterion that could not be evaluated until the adapter it might select had been built, which is why F1 now includes the comparison arm.

alternatives.option: Start the skeleton immediately and measure later
alternatives.tradeoff: Visible progress sooner; a negative F1, F3 or F5 result forces rework of the ingest port, the scheduler, the capture writer or the meeting schema.

alternatives.option: Run the gates and decide acceptance after seeing the numbers
alternatives.tradeoff: Avoids arguing about thresholds in advance; invites fitting the threshold to the result.

alternatives.option: Record ranges without their basis
alternatives.tradeoff: Less text; the owner approving them cannot tell a derived criterion from an invented one.

alternatives.option: Treat the unknowns as risks accepted at implementation time
alternatives.tradeoff: No gates to schedule; hands behavioral decisions to whichever task hits them.

decisions.consequences: Some work produces evidence rather than shippable behavior, including a measurement-only comparison harness that is not part of the product. Gate outputs feed D-001, D-004, D-009, D-011, D-020, D-023, D-027, D-028, D-030 and D-037, so those decisions carry conservative defaults until the evidence lands. Approving ranges before the work adds a decision point to the schedule.
decisions.reconsider_when: A gate's fallback proves acceptable enough that the measurement is not worth its cost, which is a judgment to record instead of assume.

decisions.title: Named approval authority, specification traceability, and approved ranges with recorded basis
decisions.choice: Expected behavior lives in docs/behavior/ tables whose rows each cite a SPEC.md clause or are marked derived. The normative approver is the user as product owner, or a delegate named in docs/behavior/OWNERS. The same approver signs each gate's range, its recorded basis and its failure action before that gate runs, and the rubric scoring rule before the fidelity corpus is scored. Approval of a table gates writing tests against it; tests reference row identifiers; changing an approved row requires re-approval recorded in git history. Independent authorship is a hygiene rule and carries no authority.
decisions.rationale: A passing test proves only that the code met its assertions, so the assertions need an owner who can say they are the intended product behavior. Ranges are part of what gets approved because they decide which runtime and which defaults ship, and each carries its basis so the approver can distinguish a criterion derived from a design parameter, such as two chunk periods or the credit-window slope, from a product target with nothing behind it, such as a latency figure.

alternatives.option: Peer review by any team member
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap and fast; two people can share the same misreading with nobody empowered to settle it.

alternatives.option: Approve behavior tables but leave measurement thresholds to engineering
alternatives.tradeoff: Less product-owner time; the thresholds deciding which defaults ship would have no product authority behind them.

alternatives.option: Treat SPEC.md as the only source and skip behavior tables
alternatives.tradeoff: No second artifact to maintain; the specification does not enumerate state and event pairs, so implementers fill the gaps silently.

alternatives.option: Derive expectations from the implementation and review the diff
alternatives.tradeoff: Least documentation work; makes the code its own specification.

decisions.consequences: Capability areas cannot be accepted until their tables are approved, and gates cannot run until their ranges are, which puts the product owner on the critical path twice. Derived rows and unbased ranges are visible as categories, so the volume of behavior and of thresholds with no specification or measurement basis stays measurable.
decisions.reconsider_when: Approval becomes the dominant delay, which would argue for pre-approved templates for mechanical tables instead of removing the gate.

decisions.title: Distribution: direct Developer ID distribution, ad hoc signing for local builds
decisions.choice: The application ships outside the Mac App Store, notarized under a Developer ID certificate with the hardened runtime, as an unsandboxed shell containing sandboxed XPC services. Local development builds may be ad hoc signed. App Store submission is not planned.
decisions.rationale: This is settled here rather than left as a blocking question because the specification decides it in substance: it asks for direct distribution for this worked example, and it requires a consuming session-level event tap with key-up for push-to-talk (D-026) and setting selected text in another application's accessibility element (D-009), neither of which is available to a sandboxed App Store build. The alternative would not satisfy requirements the specification names.

alternatives.option: Mac App Store distribution
alternatives.tradeoff: System-managed updates and a familiar install path; the sandbox removes push-to-talk and accessibility insertion as specified, so those requirements would have to be rewritten.

alternatives.option: Unsigned distribution
alternatives.tradeoff: No certificate cost; Gatekeeper blocks casual installation and every TCC grant becomes fragile.

alternatives.option: Both an App Store build and a direct build
alternatives.tradeoff: Reach plus capability; two feature sets, two permission models and two test matrices for one application.

decisions.consequences: Updates need their own mechanism, and the project carries certificate management and a notarization step in release packaging. Ad hoc signed local builds have an unstable code identity, so TCC grants for Accessibility, Input Monitoring, Screen Recording and Automation are re-requested after rebuilds; developers keep a stably signed build for permission-dependent work, documented rather than discovered. The entitlement sets in D-003 and D-028 are available because the build is not App Store sandboxed.
decisions.reconsider_when: A product decision requires App Store presence, which would require revising the Text delivery and Recording controls requirements first.

decisions.title: Notes as a separate run pinning content-addressed speaker assignments
decisions.choice: A diarization result is immutable, and assignment revision 1 commits with it. The mapping from segment to named speaker lives in speaker_assignment_revisions, an append-only chain per recording, each revision content-addressed over its assignments and naming its diarization result; identity display names are append-only in speaker_identity_names. Notes are generated by a notes run created after those inputs commit, whose manifest pins the transcript result, the diarization result, the assignment revision and the identity-name set hash, with the first three also in result_dependencies. History compares pinned identifiers against current state and reports drift with a regenerate action that creates another notes run.
decisions.rationale: Notes are the artifact whose meaning depends on user-editable data, so the snapshot rule D-006 applies to mode settings extends to assignments and names. The previous revision put noting inside the meeting run, whose manifest is fsynced at arming, so the values it claimed to pin did not exist when the manifest was written and recovery from noting had nothing authoritative to read; making notes a run that starts after its inputs commit is what makes the pin real. Content addressing makes a revision comparable across runs, and append-only names let the transcript view show what a note saw at generation time.

alternatives.option: Noting as a stage of the meeting run with a manifest extension
alternatives.tradeoff: One run per meeting; the manifest stops being a single fsynced snapshot and recovery must reason about which extension was durable.

alternatives.option: Mutable assignments with no revisions
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest editing model; a note's provenance stops describing the data that produced it as soon as a name changes.

alternatives.option: Copy the assignment into the notes result params
alternatives.tradeoff: One place to look; the copy is not comparable to current state, so History cannot say what changed.

alternatives.option: Regenerate notes automatically when assignments change
alternatives.tradeoff: Notes always current; silently replaces text the user may have relied on and spends model time on every rename.

decisions.consequences: A meeting produces at least two runs and the detail view groups them. Every speaker edit writes a revision; the rows are small and are deleted with the recording. A crash between the diarization commit and the notes run leaves a Generate action rather than a note. Assignment revisions must be reconciled when a new diarization run produces different boundaries, which carries assigned_by_user states forward where segments overlap and marks the rest unattributed.
decisions.reconsider_when: F5 shows segment identifiers are not stable enough across runs for overlap-based carry-forward, which would need a time-range mapping instead.

decisions.title: Model installation lifecycle states bound storage when a runtime is replaced
decisions.choice: model_installations carries a lifecycle state in {installed, archived, orphaned_runtime, missing}. Archiving releases the weight assets while retaining the row, the manifest and per-asset hashes, declared capabilities and the notices under Models/notices. History results keep referencing archived installations and render from results.params_rendered, and the detail view states that reprocessing needs the assets restored by import or download. Removing an adapter moves its installations to orphaned_runtime, which keeps the assets on disk, lists them with their size and an archive action, and posts a launch-time notice; nothing is deleted without a user action. Garbage collection removes assets only when no installed or orphaned_runtime row references them and no lease is live. A pinned run against an archived installation is refused up front with a restore offer.
decisions.rationale: Reference counting alone cannot bound storage, because History results reference their installations permanently, so no row is ever unreferenced and successive runtime replacements would accumulate every old model. Separating what must persist for attribution, which is small, from what must persist for execution, which is gigabytes, makes bounded storage achievable without breaking provenance. Removing an adapter is not the same event as deciding to discard weights, so it changes a state and surfaces a choice rather than deleting.

alternatives.option: Retain assets for any installation any result references
alternatives.tradeoff: Reprocessing always available; storage grows without bound across replacements.

alternatives.option: Delete assets when an adapter is removed
alternatives.tradeoff: Bounded automatically; destroys reprocessing capability on a build change the user did not make.

alternatives.option: Delete the installation row with the assets
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest cleanup; old History rows lose the identity, licences and parameters that made them attributable.

alternatives.option: Archive automatically by age or size
alternatives.tradeoff: No user decision needed; removes reprocessing without warning.

decisions.consequences: Four installation states appear in the model manager and in History, and users must understand that an archived model is attributable but not runnable while an orphaned one is present but unusable until its adapter returns. Restoring requires the same assets by manifest hash, which the retained row makes checkable. Missing is distinguished from archived so an unexpected disappearance is reported as an error rather than a user choice.
decisions.reconsider_when: Users archive and restore the same installations repeatedly, which would argue for a compressed local cache of recent weights instead of full release.

decisions.title: Retained context as an owned artifact with a stated lifetime
decisions.choice: When a mode opts into context retention, the sample is stored as a file under Recordings/<uuid>/context/<sampleId>.txt with a retained_context row naming run, recording, source kind, representation, path, byte length and SHA-256. The file is fsynced before the transaction that inserts the row, both are removed by ordinary deletion and by retention policies, the text is not added to the FTS index, and migrations own the table like any other. Without the opt-in only the digest row exists.
decisions.rationale: The previous revision promised retained context in the interface while the schema listed digests only, which left the owner, the deletion rule and the migration path to whichever implementation task first stored a string. That is exactly the deferral the specification prohibits for persistent data. Files rather than columns because screen recognition output can be large and because deletion then rides on the same directory removal as audio. Excluding it from the search index keeps History results about the user's own speech rather than about documents that happened to be open.

alternatives.option: Store retained context as a column on the run
alternatives.tradeoff: One fewer file kind; large samples inflate the database and its backup and migration times.

alternatives.option: Index retained context in FTS
alternatives.tradeoff: Search finds the surrounding material; searches return hits in text the user never spoke or wrote.

alternatives.option: Do not retain context at all
alternatives.tradeoff: Least storage and the simplest privacy story; reprocessing an old recording cannot reproduce its original result even when the user wants that.

alternatives.option: Encrypt retained context separately
alternatives.tradeoff: Stronger at-rest protection for the most sensitive sample; inconsistent with the audio and transcripts beside it, which would give false assurance.

decisions.consequences: Retention is visible in the library size view and in the per-recording detail. A mode that retains context makes each run larger, which the mode editor states when the option is enabled. Protection is the file system's, as for the rest of the library.
decisions.reconsider_when: A threat model asks for at-rest encryption, which would apply to the library as a whole rather than to context alone.

coverage.explanation: Global toggle and push-to-talk from another application come from one session-level event tap that observes key-up and consumes the hotkey (D-026), available because of the distribution decision in D-036. Toggle and push-to-talk are separate configurable bindings validated at bind time, so a press has one meaning; per-mode bindings select a mode and start a run in one action. A lost key-up is recovered from tap-disabled and screen-lock notifications and from polling the physical key state, so there is no maximum hold and no duration cap. Capture starts at the trigger into a pre-roll ring while arming runs concurrently (D-006), so a user who speaks immediately does not lose the first word, and the residual device-start latency is measured by the leading-audio test. Without Accessibility or Input Monitoring the tap cannot run, so toggle falls back to a Carbon hotkey and push-to-talk is unavailable with an explanation (D-032). Cancellation has a defined effect at every stage a run can occupy, including sealing, diarizing and noting (D-007), and sealing's effect is bounded by the backlog rule in D-004 rather than by an unstated assumption about scheduling. A crash mid-run resolves through the state-indexed recovery contract, which covers the same stage set and the meeting-without-notes case (D-031).

The processed transcript is inserted at the caret or over the current selection by setting AXSelectedText; the app never sets an element's whole value, so existing field contents survive (D-009), following the distinction RESEARCH draws between an accessibility object's value and its selected text. D-008 resolves exactly one target per focus outcome and then revalidates the frontmost process, window and focused element immediately before every posted event and before the submit Return, because those events reach whatever is focused when they are posted and processing can take seconds; a mismatch ends the attempt as unconfirmed. Fallthrough is rung-specific, which is what prevents duplicate delivery: an accessibility error is returned before any effect and permits the paste rung, while an unchanged readback after Command-V is not a rejection, since a delayed consumer can apply the paste afterwards, so synthesized typing runs only when a target-specific rejection signal recorded in that target's profile fires. Every other outcome is a content-based confirmation or an unconfirmed stop. Optional submission posts Return after a confirmed delivery to a revalidated target, whichever rung achieved it, so the preferred accessibility path supports submission. Clipboard changes are handled by snapshotting before writing and restoring only after confirmed delivery while the change count is ours, or on the user's action; there is no timer, and after an unconfirmed outcome the transcript stays on the clipboard and the panel says so. Permissions denied or revoked route the result to History and the clipboard through the capability matrix (D-032), and secure input suppresses synthesis. Duplicate delivery is prevented structurally: the attempt row and per-rung records commit before any effect, delivered is terminal, and only pending, in_progress and unconfirmed become needs_review at launch (D-010).

A provisional live transcript comes from a pass over a sliding window and a waveform is drawn from a 10 ms RMS and peak envelope computed allocation-free on the capture thread (D-011). The compact window is a non-activating, borderless panel at status-bar level that joins all spaces, is movable by its background and never becomes key, so showing it cannot disturb the delivery target. Placement is remembered as a fraction of the display's visible frame plus the display identifier and clamped to the primary display when either is gone. Provisional text renders in a secondary style with a live label and is replaced by the final transcript with a change highlight; the provisional stream is never persisted, because it was produced over partial context and is a different artifact from the recognition result the run commits (D-006). Failures appear as a panel row with a short reason and one action. The ladder that keeps provisional text available is now executable rather than nominal: an interactive run reserves the speech-primary slot and preempts batch speech work (D-004), and a preview-class installation under 400 MB has its own slot in the budget (D-027), so the fallback rungs do not queue behind a long import. Each rung has stated criteria for first-text latency, update interval, dropped frames and final-transcript quality, measured in F1's preview arm. Waveform-only is not an accepted end state, because provisional text is a named requirement; if no rung meets its criteria on the evaluation target, that is a release question for the product owner.

Four built-in modes cover ordinary dictation and task-specific output: Standard, Email, Note and Meeting notes (D-013), each carrying a structured contract rather than a prose description. Standard is limited to punctuation, capitalization, optional disfluency removal and vocabulary substitution; Email adds template salutation and sign-off, paragraph structure and register adjustment with no new factual content; Note adds list and heading structure; Meeting notes permits summarization because that is its purpose and is bounded by a citation requirement in place of a recall threshold. All four declare that they do not answer questions, and what the design claims about that declaration is bounded by what its checks establish (D-012). The language-independent set always runs, covering expansion ratio, context overlap, vocabulary survival and script sanity, with orthographic question-mark detection reported as a signal. Where a validator pack exists, the language-dependent set checks interrogative survival in order, content-word recall and unsupported sentences. An observed violation retries once with a stricter instruction and then delivers the normalized transcript while retaining the generated text marked contract_violation. Where no pack exists, the rewrite is produced and retained but the delivered text is the normalized transcript, because the check that protects the declaration is the one missing and a question-mark signal cannot establish that no question was asked; there is no setting that overrides this, since the specification requires answering to be explicitly part of the selected mode. These checks are necessary conditions, not proof of fidelity, which is why the adversarial corpus and the rubric rule in verification decide whether a built-in ships.

Users author prompts and formatting rules, and each custom mode fills in a structured contract naming its allowed operations, whether it may answer questions, its content bound, the languages its validator supports and the representation of each context source; the editor cannot save a mode without one, because a free-form prompt gives the checker nothing to check against (D-012). Each mode selects its own local speech and language models by content identity rather than by name, and that identity covers every behavior-affecting asset (D-022). Every save creates a content-addressed revision in an append-only chain, and every run pins the revision id into its manifest at start along with model installations, runtime and adapter revisions, vocabulary revision, language and validator pack set (D-006). Work already in progress reads its snapshot and never live settings, so editing a mode or updating a runtime during a recognition cannot change what the running job produces, and a saved result keeps pointing at the revision and the code revision that produced it. History names the producing revision and diffs it against the current one. Because every result also names its run and its inputs (D-029), a rewrite produced by an old revision stays attributable after the audio is recognized again under a different model. Check coverage never restricts model choice: a mode may select any compatible installation in any language, the rewrite is always produced and retained, and what varies is which checks ran and whether the rewrite is delivered automatically.

Rules match the foreground application's bundle identifier and, where readable, the website URL, evaluated at arming with first match winning over a user-ordered list (D-014). List position is the complete precedence rule, so the answer is readable off the list from top to bottom; specificity only proposes an insertion point in the editor and flags rules an earlier rule shadows, which is why no priority field exists to be tie-broken against. When a predicate's input cannot be obtained, because browser automation is denied, the browser exposes no URL, or screen recording is off, rules needing that input do not match and evaluation continues; if nothing matches, the user's default mode applies. Permission loss is handled per capability, so losing browser automation narrows rule matching without disturbing capture or recognition (D-032). The chosen mode is latched into the run manifest, so it cannot change mid-sentence, and the effective mode plus whether it came from a rule or the fallback appears in the recording panel and the menu bar for every run, which is what keeps the current mode apparent (D-011). Which browsers expose a URL is enumerated in a dated matrix before URL rules ship, and an incomplete matrix degrades to bundle-identifier rules.

User terminology and names enter at four points with a fixed order relative to recognition and language processing (D-015). Before recognition, selected terms go into the decoder's prompt slot, bounded by the runtime's limit and chosen by mode relevance and recency; that shifts decoding probabilities and the interface says exactly that, with no claim that adding a name guarantees recognition, because the mechanism is a prompt rather than a decoding constraint (D-020). After recognition, replacements run deterministically over the recognition result with an explicit match precedence: longest match at each position, ties broken by list order, boundary-aware using ICU segmentation for the run's language, case-preserving, non-overlapping and applied once with no cascading, so two implementations cannot produce different normalized transcripts while satisfying the same prose. Where segmentation is unavailable the pipeline falls back to substring matching with a warning in the editor. Filler removal is a separate per-mode pass. After generation the table is applied once more, and vocabulary survival is a language-independent check, so it runs whether or not a pack exists (D-012); a model that normalizes an unusual proper noun back to a common word is caught and the user's spelling wins. Recognition and normalized results are both retained, so the effect of each stage is inspectable.

Three optional sources are sampled at arming in parallel against a 200 ms deadline: focused-element text, selection and window title through accessibility; one frame of the focused window through ScreenCaptureKit with Vision text recognition when opted in; and the first text item on the pasteboard, each capped (D-016). Sampling once at arming bounds cost and makes a run reproducible, and anything missing the deadline is omitted and recorded as omitted. Context is data supplied to a mode, and the design now treats every source the same way: all three are distilled to a capped term list before reaching the prompt, which removes instruction-shaped sentences rather than detecting them afterwards, and the earlier asymmetry that always passed focused-element text as prose is gone, since a focused field can hold text someone else wrote. A mode may opt a source into prose, and then automatic delivery additionally requires the language-dependent check set to be available and to pass; otherwise the normalized transcript is delivered and the generated text is held (D-012). The residual limit is stated rather than papered over: an instruction obeyed in words absent from the context is not detectable by any listed check, and what bounds the damage is that the transcript is preserved and delivery is the only automatic external effect. Retention defaults to a digest, and opting in stores an owned artifact with a row, a path and deletion rules that ride on the recording (D-039). Every transient copy has a release point, including the assembled prompt in both processes, and no inference service writes prompts or context to disk. Missing permissions leave a named operating state (D-032), and context never leaves the machine because it crosses only an XPC connection to a service the system denies network access (D-028).

Recognition language is set per mode to an explicit code or to detection using the runtime's language identification with its probability; below the threshold the run records undetermined, uses the mode's default and the panel says so (D-017). Translation into English is a separate declared operation that inserts a result naming the exact recognition or normalized result it translated, so the source transcript is preserved beside any derived text and stays identifiable after the same audio is recognized again under a different model (D-029). Recognition and rewriting are evaluated by different methods and reported separately, word error rate for the first and a scored human rubric for the second, because a rewrite score cannot distinguish a mis-recognized word from a badly reworded sentence. Compatibility is declared per installation and checked against the per-kind runtime descriptor at activation (D-022); the interface attributes language claims to the model publisher and marks them unmeasured until an evaluation row exists. Pack coverage restricts neither which models may be used nor which languages may be recognized or rewritten: without a pack the model runs, the result is produced, retained and searchable, and the language-independent checks still apply. What a missing pack changes is the automatic delivery of a rewrite for a mode that declares it does not answer questions, where the normalized transcript is delivered and the rewrite is one click away, which is a property of the mode's own declaration rather than a limit on the model (D-012).

Microphone, system audio and imported audio and video all implement one AudioSource emitting native-format frames carrying stream id, clock domain, presentation time, sequence and a discontinuity flag, with conversion to the canonical 16 kHz mono input as an explicit stage after the port (D-018). Consumers grant credit, so a seekable source stops decoding when the recognizer falls behind and a live source that overruns records a discontinuity rather than buffering without bound; credit extends across the service connection, which bounds memory in both processes. The initial format matrix is what the system decoders cover: wav, aiff, caf, mp3, m4a in AAC and ALAC, mp4, m4v and mov. The extension mechanism is a DecoderProvider port with an opt-in external command-line decoder, off by default, run as a child of the sandboxed decode service; whether it inherits the restriction is tested directly at F2, and if it does not, it stays off by default with the trust transfer stated (D-028). Concurrency is now bounded rather than implied: one live capture session at a time, and seekable ingest occupies one of a bounded number of ingest slots, so several imports cannot each hold windows, journals and buffers outside the budget, while live capture writing and sealing stay exempt from admission because deferring a live source loses audio (D-004). Files decode in 30-second windows, and the memory claim is tested as a slope across 10-minute, 1-hour and 3-hour imports in both processes. A failed import leaves its source unchanged because the path opens it read-only, copies into the session directory and commits only after the artifact is complete; on failure the directory is removed and no row exists (D-019).

A meeting captures microphone and system audio as two artifacts whose frames carry host-time stamps, so alignment and gaps are represented by the ingest port rather than reconstructed afterwards (D-018), with a stated drift range and a tone-derived correction, and capture is crash-safe through the chunk journal and its idempotent finalization (D-030). Channel origin is recorded as a fact about capture and labeled as the microphone channel and the system audio channel; it is not presented as speaker identity, because a microphone can pick up remote audio and a system stream can carry several applications (D-023). Speaker separation has an explicit runtime and an explicit home: SpeakerKit's Pyannote pipeline behind a Diarizer port in its own sandboxed DiarizationService with download disabled, an explicit model folder and explicit concurrency recorded in the manifest, with weights acquired by the user. Diarization is a run stage with a cancellation effect, a recovery transition and admission accounting, and its model set counts against the residency budget alongside speech, preview and generation (D-006, D-027). Evidence is represented at the boundary the cited declaration supports: per-segment calibrated confidence is unknown, no per-segment margin is stored, and centroid distance proposes cross-recording identity for confirmation rather than applying it. Segments default to unverified and notes attribute only assigned segments. Editing names appends an assignment revision and a name entry, and notes are a separate run created after the diarization result and revision 1 commit, pinning all of them in a manifest fsynced at that run's start and in dependency rows that can name an assignment revision, so a later rename or re-diarization cannot change what a saved note meant while History reports the drift and offers regeneration (D-037, D-029). Timestamped notes cite segment ranges and drop uncited bullets. F5 inventories the fields the pinned SDK exposes before the schema freezes, and diarization quality is measured with a range that decides the shipped default rather than the feature's availability.

Recordings are searchable through FTS5 over result text with bm25 ranking and snippets, and playable from the sealed artifact (D-005, D-024). Each recording expands into its processing runs, and each run into a result chain rooted at that run's recognition or diarization result, so reprocessing through another model or mode inserts a new run and new results while every earlier result stays immutable and attributable (D-029). The relationship between original audio and successive results is one recording to many runs to many results, each naming its primary input, its other inputs by role and kind, the mode revision, the model installations and the runtime and adapter revisions that produced it. A user-movable pointer selects the displayed run. Deletion while processing is active sets a tombstone, increments a generation counter and signals cancellation; every worker carries the recording id and generation from admission and commits in one transaction that aborts if the row is missing, tombstoned or at a different generation, so a late response cannot recreate a deleted recording because the check and the insert cannot be separated. Deletion requested before the sealing commit is a manifest disposition, since no row exists to tombstone (D-033). Retention is not a separate mechanism: age, size and audio-discarding policies acquire the same leases, skip recordings held by a live holder, and move audio to a discarded state that disables playback, re-recognition and re-diarization while leaving text reprocessing available. A lease is reclaimed only when its holder is provably gone, so a busy or suspended holder cannot have its artifact deleted underneath it. Interrupted work resolves through the state-indexed recovery contract, which covers diarizing and noting (D-031), and space is reported as deleting until the last lease releases.

The model library browses and manages installed speech, preview, language and diarization models with their capabilities, sizes, per-asset licences and owning runtime (D-022). Identity is publisher, revision string and a hash over a manifest covering every behavior-affecting asset, including tokenizer, configuration and template, and each run additionally records the runtime and adapter revision, so a result names what produced it including the code. Compatibility and the smoke test are per kind, so a diarizer missing its clusterer or a speech model missing its tokenizer fails at install rather than mid-run; that test is a capability check and never a quality judgment, so a compatible model with no benchmark row activates normally and is labeled unmeasured, and the evaluation harness with its ranges is development tooling for shipped defaults that gates nothing in the application (D-034). Installation stages, verifies, smoke-tests, then renames into an immutable content-addressed directory, after which one transaction records the installation and moves the active pointer; a crash between those steps leaves an unreferenced blob that collection removes, and a run pinned to the previous installation holds a lease. A failed download or import cannot replace a working installation. Model loading never triggers a download: runtimes receive absolute paths through one of three access mechanisms, initializers that can fetch are prohibited by a build check, acquisition is confined to an explicitly invoked downloader on a host allowlist, and all four inference services are denied the network by their sandbox, with no fallback outside that boundary (D-028, D-003, D-023). Replacing a runtime has bounded effect on interface and storage: runtimes are separate adapter targets and service binaries with their own descriptors and parameter schemas (D-002, D-020, D-021), old rows render from params_rendered after an adapter is removed, removing an adapter marks installations orphaned_runtime without deleting anything, and archiving releases assets while retaining identity, hashes and notices, which are stored outside the blob so archiving cannot delete them (D-038). Activation exceeding the residency budget, which counts speech, preview, generation and diarization together with a stated non-model floor, is refused with the arithmetic shown, labeled measured or declared, and overridable (D-027).

A menu bar status item is the always-available surface showing state, effective mode, recent results and settings, complementing the recording panel (D-011, D-025). Microphone level adjustment is software gain on captured buffers by default, with metering and a clipping indicator, so the common case changes no system state and has nothing to restore; setting the input device's hardware volume is opt-in and restored only if the current value still equals what the app set, with any mismatch leaving the setting as found and saying so. Media control is confined to what the app can own: an adapter identifies the player, issues a one-way pause to it and observes the transition to paused, and only such a pause is resumed automatically, and only while the player still reports paused and nothing else has changed it. For a player with no adapter the app takes no automatic action at all, because the media key is a toggle that can start a paused player while an unrelated client keeps the output device active; Pause media and Resume playback are offered as explicit user actions labeled with that uncertainty. Competing applications and manual user edits therefore produce no automatic restoration and a note that playback or the setting was left as found. Losing automation permission for a player removes its adapter and drops that player to the manual actions (D-032). The macOS baseline and the public APIs these behaviors use are set by D-001, with anything newer behind an availability check and a defined fallback.

open_questions.question: Which of the three access mechanisms does each runtime need to load its models inside a sandboxed service with the network entitlement withheld, and does the external decoder the decode service spawns inherit the restriction?
open_questions.resolution: Gate F2, before the entitlement set and access path are frozen. Load each model kind by descriptor passing, by a read-only path exception scoped to Models/blobs, and by materialization inside the service's own container; attempt outbound connections and a write outside the job scratch directory and assert both fail; repeat from the spawned decoder. This was argued to be blocking while a failed mechanism could move a runtime outside the sandbox; that fallback is removed in D-028, so F2 no longer decides the trust boundary. It selects a mechanism, and if a runtime loads under none of them the alternative adapter behind the same port is used. Only the case where a required model kind has no adapter that loads inside the boundary reaches the product owner, and it would be a specification question rather than an implementation choice.

open_questions.question: How does the shipping speech runtime behave on long input and under cancellation, and does it meet the accuracy, latency and memory ranges for the default pairing?
open_questions.resolution: Gate F1, with ranges, bases and failure actions approved under D-035 before it runs. F1 builds a measurement-only whisper.cpp harness alongside the shipping adapter so the retention comparison is executable rather than dependent on first shipping the adapter it might select, and it defines an equivalent model as the same upstream checkpoint at the nearest available quantization in each format. It also measures cancellation latency, checkpoint equivalence and the preview arm. Failure of a range promotes the harness to a shipping adapter or changes the default model size, both of which satisfy the same requirement.

open_questions.question: How much captured audio is lost when the writer is killed at an arbitrary offset, does finalization survive a crash at every one of its write boundaries, and does the sealer hold its backlog bound under contention?
open_questions.resolution: Gate F3, before recovery expectations for capturing and sealing are approved. Kill the writer at randomized offsets across chunk boundaries, at both per-chunk fsync points and at every finalization write, and kill again during recovery, asserting a maximum lost interval of at most 4 seconds, a decodable artifact whose packet count matches the durable prefix, and convergence of repeated recovery. Separately measure the backlog with a concurrent import and a loaded CPU. If the interval is exceeded, shorten the chunk period; if reconstruction is ever invalid, retain journal chunks until the finalized artifact decodes and hashes; if the backlog exceeds its bound, the shed sequence in D-004 already defines the behavior and the encode cost is reduced.

open_questions.question: Which insertion paths preserve existing field content, which targets allow the confirmation predicate to be evaluated, and which expose a rejection signal that would justify a synthesized-typing entry in their delivery profile?
open_questions.resolution: Gate F4, before delivery profiles ship. Prototype rung 1 and rung 2 with readback in the applications listed under verification, recording content survival, predicate evaluability, any rejection signal, pasteboard read timing and snapshot cost by content type. The ladder does not wait on the table: with no profile entry, synthesized typing is unreachable and an unevaluable outcome is unconfirmed with the transcript left on the pasteboard. The table adds safe fallthrough where evidence supports it and sets the snapshot limit from data.

open_questions.question: Which fields does the pinned SpeakerKit version expose in DiarizationResult, which speakers receive centroids on multi-speaker fixtures, what do the segmenter and embedder cost in resident size and wall time, and do the download flag and model folder suppress acquisition under a network-denied profile?
open_questions.resolution: Gate F5, a thin adapter experiment before the meeting schema and diarization residency numbers freeze. RESEARCH establishes centroid embeddings with cosine-distance helpers and establishes that per-segment confidence and margin are not exposed, so the schema already stores unknown for those; F5 confirms the field list at the pinned version and supplies the numbers admission needs. The structural fallbacks are recorded: no centroid means cross-recording naming for that speaker is a user action with no proposal, and unstable segment identifiers move assignment carry-forward to time-range overlap (D-037).

open_questions.question: Which languages get validator packs at ship, and how often does a missing pack withhold automatic delivery from users who wanted the rewrite?
open_questions.resolution: Ship the English pack with the first generation modes and add packs driven by the measured checks_partial and one-click delivery rates per language. No model or language is blocked in the meantime, and the rewrite is always produced and retained, so the cost of a missing pack is measurable rather than assumed. A mode intended for an unpacked language can be authored as a revision declaring that it answers questions, which the mode indicator shows.

open_questions.question: Which browsers expose the current URL through accessibility, and which need automation permission or provide nothing?
open_questions.resolution: Enumerate per browser and record a dated table before URL rules ship. The rule engine treats an unreadable URL as a non-match, so an incomplete table degrades to bundle-identifier rules and the default mode.

open_questions.question: Is FTS5 compiled into the system SQLite on the chosen baseline?
open_questions.resolution: A runtime check during store setup. If absent, build GRDB against a bundled SQLite, accepting a larger binary and an update obligation, and record the change against D-005.

open_questions.question: Is an 8B-class instruct model at 4-bit quantization the right default for Email and Meeting notes on the 16 GB target, given that a preview model and diarization now share the budget?
open_questions.resolution: Score two or three sizes against the fidelity corpus under the approved rubric rule, recording violation and checks_partial rates per model, and pair the result with the F5 diarization footprint and the preview slot so the recommended default fits the budget with meetings running. Model selection is per mode either way, so a wrong default is a settings change.

open_questions.question: Which rung of the preview ladder meets its first-text latency, update interval, dropped-frame and final-quality criteria on the evaluation target?
open_questions.resolution: F1's preview arm measures capture with the primary streaming pass, then with a preview-class model in its own slot, then with batched updates at voice-activity pauses. The highest rung that passes ships. If none passes, that is a release question for the product owner under D-035 rather than a removal of provisional text, because the requirement names it (D-011).

open_questions.question: Which diarization weight assets may be offered for download rather than only imported?
open_questions.resolution: Compile the notice inventory per asset against the component-specific references RESEARCH records for the embedder and clusterer, and store each notice under Models/notices so archiving cannot remove it. The feature ships either way, because weights are user-acquired through the model store and an asset whose notice does not permit redistribution stays importable; the inventory decides only what the downloader offers.
